propositions.text: The Applicant seeks judicial review of a decision rejecting his application for permanent residence on humanitarian and compassionate grounds under section 25(1) IRPA.
propositions.quote: The Applicant seeks judicial review of a decision rejecting his application for permanent residence on humanitarian and compassionate (H&C) grounds, pursuant to section 25(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 (IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant seeks judicial review of a decision rejecting his permanent residence application on humanitarian and compassionate grounds under section 25(1) IRPA, court states.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is dismissed.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, the application is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application for judicial review.

propositions.text: The Applicant is a Sunni Muslim who claimed protection fearing persecution by Shia extremists and government, rejected on credibility grounds by RPD and RAD.
propositions.quote: The Applicant is a Sunni Muslim. He was working at the Baghdad airport as an engineer and came to Canada on November 1, 2015. He made a claim for protection on the grounds that he feared persecution at the hands of Shia extremist groups and the Shia government because he is Sunni and from Daesh or ISIS on the basis that he was a moderate and not religious enough. His claim was rejected by the Refugee Protection Division on credibility grounds in December 2016. An appeal to the Refugee Appeal Division was denied in August 2017.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant is a Sunni Muslim whose refugee claim was rejected on credibility grounds by RPD and RAD, court states.

propositions.text: The Applicant remains in Canada due to Temporary Suspension of Removals and is employed supporting his parents who also lack status.
propositions.quote: The Applicant has remained in Canada due to the Temporary Suspension of Removals (TSR) to Iraq and these proceedings. He has been employed on a work permit as an industrial mechanic. He is supporting his parents who arrived in Canada in 2017 and also do not have status.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant remains in Canada under TSR, employed and supporting his parents who also lack status, court states.

propositions.text: The H&C application was submitted in August 2018 and refused on October 1, 2020, based on establishment, family ties, and hardship in Iraq.
propositions.quote: The application for permanent residence on H&C grounds was submitted in August 2018 and refused on October 1, 2020. It was based on establishment in Canada, family ties to Canada and hardship the Applicant would face in Iraq.

paragraphs.summary: The H&C application was submitted in 2018 and refused in 2020 based on establishment, family ties, and hardship, court states.

propositions.text: The issue is whether the Officer’s decision is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: There is one issue to be addressed on this application: Is the Officer’s decision unreasonable?

paragraphs.summary: The issue is whether the Officer’s decision is unreasonable, court states.

propositions.text: The Applicant submits the standard of review is reasonableness.
propositions.quote: The Applicant and the Respondent submit that the standard of review is reasonableness.

propositions.text: The Respondent submits the standard of review is reasonableness.
propositions.quote: The Applicant and the Respondent submit that the standard of review is reasonableness.

propositions.text: Reasonableness is the presumptive standard for judicial review per Vavilov, avoiding undue interference with administrative decision makers.
propositions.quote: As determined by the Supreme Court of Canada in Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov] at para 30, reasonableness is the presumptive standard for most categories of questions on judicial review, a presumption that avoids undue interference with the administrative decision maker’s discharge of its functions.

propositions.text: No circumstances arise here to set aside the presumption of reasonableness standard.
propositions.quote: While there are circumstances in which the presumption can be set aside, as discussed in Vavilov, none of them arise in the present case.

paragraphs.summary: Both parties submit the standard of review is reasonableness; court agrees citing Vavilov and finds no reason to set aside this presumption.

propositions.text: Reasonableness review focuses on the actual decision and its justification per Vavilov.
propositions.quote: The court conducting a reasonableness review must focus on the decision the administrative decision maker actually made (Vavilov at para 15), including the justification offered for it.

propositions.text: Reasonableness requires justification, transparency, intelligibility, and defensibility in facts and law per Vavilov and Dunsmuir.
propositions.quote: To determine whether the decision is reasonable, the reviewing court must ask “whether the decision bears the hallmarks of reasonableness – justification, transparency and intelligibility – and whether it is justified in relation to the relevant factual and legal constraints that bear on the decision” (Vavilov at paras 86 and 99). Thus, decision-maker's findings should not be disturbed as long as the decision “falls within a range of possible, acceptable outcomes which are defensible in respect of the facts and law” (Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9, at para 47).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the reasonableness standard requires justification, transparency, intelligibility, and defensibility of the decision per Vavilov and Dunsmuir.

propositions.text: Deference is owed to factual findings; court must not reweigh evidence or importance of factors per Kanthasamy and Vavilov.
propositions.quote: In conducting a reasonableness review of factual findings, deference is warranted and it is not the role of the Court to reweigh the evidence or the relative importance given by the decision-maker to any relevant factor (Kanthasamy v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 SCC 61 [Kanthasamy] at para 112; Vavilov at para 96)

propositions.text: The party challenging the decision bears the burden to show unreasonableness per Vavilov.
propositions.quote: The party challenging the decision bears the burden of showing that it is unreasonable (Vavilov at para 100).

paragraphs.summary: The court states deference is owed to factual findings and the challenger bears the burden to prove unreasonableness, citing Kanthasamy and Vavilov.

propositions.text: Not all errors warrant intervention; only serious shortcomings affecting justification, intelligibility, transparency justify intervention per Vavilov and Mason.
propositions.quote: Not all errors or concerns about a decision will warrant intervention. To intervene, the reviewing court must be satisfied that there are “sufficiently serious shortcomings” in the decision such that it does not exhibit sufficient justification, intelligibility and transparency. Flaws or shortcomings must be more than superficial or peripheral to the merits of the decision, or a “minor misstep”. The problem must be sufficiently central or significant to render the decision unreasonable: Vavilov, at para 100; Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Mason, 2021 FCA 156, at para 36.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains only serious, central shortcomings justify intervention, not minor or superficial errors, citing Vavilov and Mason.

propositions.text: The Applicant argues the Officer used his establishment against him, misapprehended evidence on family and discounted ties to friends and colleagues.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the Officer used his successful establishment against him which undermined the hardship he would face if returned to Iraq. He contends that the Officer misapprehended or disregarded the Applicant’s evidence on his relationship with his parents, and discounted the Applicant’s ties to friends and colleagues in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the Officer used his establishment against him and disregarded evidence on family and social ties, Applicant submits.

propositions.text: An H&C officer cannot give positive weight to establishment and simultaneously use it to reduce future hardship, per Singh and Aguirre Renteria.
propositions.quote: The Court has held that an H&C officer can’t ascribe positive weight to an applicant’s establishment, on the one hand, and on the other, use it to attenuate future hardship: Singh v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 1633, at para 27; Aguirre Renteria v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 134, at para 8.

paragraphs.summary: The court states H&C officers cannot both positively weigh establishment and use it to reduce hardship, citing Singh and Aguirre Renteria.

propositions.text: The Officer found the Applicant’s establishment was common and not significantly weighty, which was reasonable.
propositions.quote: In this instance, while the Officer noted that the Applicant’s acquired skills of resiliency, drive and determination would potentially facilitate his return to Iraq, he found that the Applicant’s establishment was not uncommon for individuals who reside in Canada. It is not so out of the ordinary that it would carry significant weight. In my view, this was not an unreasonable finding.

propositions.text: Regular, ordinary establishment is neutral and should not excite a desire to relieve misfortunes, per De Sousa and Rong.
propositions.quote: As stated by Justice Roy in De Sousa v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 818 at para 28: …I fail to see how regular, ordinary establishment in Canada can be given significant weight as a decision maker must decide whether the evidence rises to the level of exciting in a reasonable person in a civilized community a desire to relieve the misfortunes of another. The fact that the establishment is not extraordinary should not be held against an applicant. It is merely neutral. The presence of establishment that is in line with reasonable expectations can hardly excite the desire to relieve the misfortunes of someone. See also: Rong v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 690, at para 32.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer reasonably concluded the Applicant’s establishment was common and neutral, citing De Sousa and Rong.

propositions.text: Officers should not create heightened standards using terms like 'exceptional' or 'extraordinary' per Damian.
propositions.quote: It has been stated that an officer should not use descriptive terms such as “exceptional and extraordinary” to create a heightened standard: Damian v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 1158 [Damian] at paras 17-21.

propositions.text: Section 25 IRPA requires applicants to establish reasons that may be described as exceptional or extraordinary relative to others, per Huang.
propositions.quote: However, s 25 of IRPA is not simply an alternative immigration scheme and an applicant has to establish reasons for why they should be allowed to remain in Canada which may fairly be described as “exceptional or extraordinary” when used in the sense of relative to other persons who apply for an exemption from the normal visa requirements Huang v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 265 [Huang] at para 20.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains officers should not create heightened standards but s 25 IRPA requires reasons that may be exceptional relative to others, citing Damian and Huang.

propositions.text: The Officer did not set a higher threshold but noted the Applicant’s establishment was ordinary and did not undermine hardship.
propositions.quote: I don’t read the Officer’s reasons in this case as setting a higher threshold but as simply noting that the Applicant’s establishment did not stand out.. The Officer noted that the Applicant had done what is reasonably expected in a common level of establishment - working, volunteering, learning the language and making friends. Nor did the Officer undermine the hardship the Applicant would face in Iraq by referring to his abilities, unlike the situation in Damian. The Officer reasonably noted that the Applicant had managed to cope with the difficulties of being a member of the Sunni minority in a Shia-dominated society in obtaining education and employment.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer reasonably noted the Applicant’s establishment was ordinary and did not undermine hardship.

propositions.text: The Officer made a minor factual error on address but acknowledged family ties and social network; parents lack status and face removal risk.
propositions.quote: The Officer made a minor factual error with respect to the Applicant’s address. It is clear that he resides with his family and supports his parents. The Officer acknowledged that the Applicant wished to live near them and weighed the family ties in his favour as well as his broader social network in Canada. However, as noted above, the parents also lack status in Canada and may themselves face removal to Iraq should their own application for judicial review of a negative H&C decision be dismissed. At present, they too benefit from the active TSR.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer made a minor address error but acknowledged family ties; parents lack status and face removal risk.

propositions.text: The Applicant contends the Officer trivialized country conditions and failed to apply Kanthasamy’s compassionate approach.
propositions.quote: The Applicant contends that the Officer trivialized conditions in a country where Canada has imposed a TSR and did not follow the compassionate approach required by Kanthasamy.

propositions.text: Kanthasamy requires showing personal effect by adverse country conditions, which Applicant failed to show to Officer’s satisfaction.
propositions.quote: But the Supreme Court in Kanthasamy,at paras 55-56, required that an applicant show that they would be personally affected by adverse country conditions which he was unable to do to the officer’s satisfaction.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the Officer trivialized country conditions and failed to apply Kanthasamy; court notes Kanthasamy requires personal effect showing.

propositions.text: A TSR must be considered when assessing personal circumstances but does not dictate a specific outcome, per Ndikumana and Likale.
propositions.quote: A TSR does not necessarily lead to a specific outcome but must be taken into account when assessing the Applicant’s personal circumstances: Ndikumana v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 328 [Ndikumana]at para 18; Likale v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 43 [Likale] at para 40.

paragraphs.summary: The court states a TSR must be considered in assessing personal circumstances but does not dictate outcome, citing Ndikumana and Likale.

propositions.text: The Officer recognized the TSR and gave it some weight but did not let it outweigh other factors; this was reasonable.
propositions.quote: The Officer recognized the active TSR to Iraq and did attribute some weight to that fact but did not find it to overweigh all of the other factors in the application. In doing so, the Officer did not minimize the conditions in Iraq but rather analyzed whether the Applicant was distinguishable from any other person in that country and required relief in Canada. An officer can give less weight to country conditions if the TSR means that an applicant will not be returning to his country in the foreseeable future and facing those conditions: Ndikumana at para 19; Likale at paras 36 and 38; Alcin v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 1242 at para 55.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer reasonably weighed the TSR and country conditions without minimizing hardship.

propositions.text: The Applicant submits the Officer disregarded evidence and used its absence to discount hardship in Iraq.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the Officer disregarded the evidence presented and used its absence in his analysis to discount the hardship the Applicant would face in Iraq.

propositions.text: The court disagrees; the Officer justified decision by citing insufficient objective evidence but did not say none was provided.
propositions.quote: I disagree. While the Officer did not refer to each item of evidence, he justified his decision by referring to “insufficient objective evidence” and did not suggest that none was provided.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the Officer disregarded evidence; the court disagrees, finding the Officer justified decision citing insufficient evidence.

propositions.text: Officer did not explicitly refer to letter from Applicant's sister about his risk if returned to Iraq
propositions.quote: The Officer did not explicitly refer to certain evidence, such as a letter from the Applicant’s sister explaining how he would be affected because of his profile should he return to Iraq.

propositions.text: Officer considered Iraq's employment rate with Applicant's education, work experience, and sibling support
propositions.quote: The Officer did consider the employment rate in Iraq and analyzed it in light of the Applicant’s education, work experience in Iraq and support to be expected from his siblings there.

propositions.text: Officer was not satisfied Applicant would be disproportionately affected upon return to Iraq
propositions.quote: With that evidence, the Officer was not satisfied that the Applicant would be disproportionately affected.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found the Officer did not mention a sister's letter but considered employment and family support, concluding no disproportionate effect on Applicant.

propositions.text: Section 25 IRPA is not relief for all from less advantageous countries
propositions.quote: Section 25 of IRPA is not a relief scheme for all who come from less advantageous countries and manage to make their way to Canada.

propositions.text: Applicants with years of work in origin country expected to have resources to readjust there
propositions.quote: It is not unreasonable to expect that when an applicant had worked for many years in his country of origin that he would have the necessary resources to readjust to life in that country: Likale at para 36.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker stated s 25 IRPA is not for all from disadvantaged countries and expects applicants with work history to readjust in origin country.

propositions.text: Applicant contends Officer failed to be sensitive to his moderate Sunni Muslim status
propositions.quote: The Applicant contends that the Officer failed to be sensitive to his status as a moderate Sunni Muslim.

propositions.text: Officer correctly identified Applicant as Sunni Muslim but missed nuance of moderate status and ISIS risk
propositions.quote: The Officer refers to the Applicant as being a practicing adherent of the Sunni branch of the religion, which is correct, but doesn’t capture the nuance of someone who may be targeted by more extremist practitioners such as the members of ISIS for not being scrupulous enough in his faith.

propositions.text: Difficult for officer to ascertain applicant's belief spectrum and its effect; flaw not central or significant
propositions.quote: In my view, it would be difficult for an officer considering a s 25 application to ascertain just where on a spectrum of belief an applicant falls and how that might affect their personal situation. To the extent that this was a flaw or shortcoming in the decision, I don’t think it was sufficiently central or significant to render the whole decision unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Officer lacked sensitivity to his moderate Sunni status; Officer noted Sunni but missed nuance; court finds this flaw not significant.

propositions.text: Officer not satisfied Applicant showed sufficient personal risk upon return to Iraq
propositions.quote: The Officer was not satisfied that the Applicant provided sufficient evidence that he will personally be at risk upon return to Iraq, especially because he used to reside in Iraq, as a Sunni Muslim, and his siblings continue to reside there.

propositions.text: Officer found discrimination from Shia majority insufficient to outweigh other factors in H&C decision
propositions.quote: While the Applicant may face some level of discrimination from members of the Shia majority and the Shia-led government, the Officer reasonably found that was insufficient to outweigh the other factors in making the H&C determination.

propositions.text: Applicant's claimed persecution risk was considered and found not credible by RPD and RAD
propositions.quote: It is perhaps worth noting again that the Applicant’s claimed risk of persecution had been considered by the RPD and RAD and found not to be credible.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found insufficient evidence of personal risk, discrimination insufficient to outweigh factors, and prior tribunals found risk not credible.

propositions.text: Officer's decision to dismiss Applicant's H&C application was reasonable and justified
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that the Officer’s decision to dismiss the Applicant’s request for permanent residence on H&C grounds was reasonable. It bore the hallmarks of reasonableness – justification, transparency and intelligibility – and was justified in relation to the relevant factual and legal constraints.

propositions.text: Decision falls within acceptable range defensible on facts and law
propositions.quote: The decision falls within the range of acceptable outcomes defensible on the facts and the law.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the Officer's dismissal of the Applicant's H&C application was reasonable and defensible on facts and law.

propositions.text: No serious questions of general importance for certification
propositions.quote: The parties offered no serious questions of general importance for certification and I am satisfied that there is none.

propositions.text: Application is dismissed and no questions certified
propositions.quote: THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that the application is dismissed. No questions are certified.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application and certifies no questions of general importance.
